| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="package.json" (Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\baileys\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\@whiskeysockets\\baileys\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/node_modules/baileys/*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/node_modules/@whiskeysockets/baileys/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
npm/yarn/pnpm install or upgrade of Baileys package AIInstallation Medium
Detects in-flight installation or upgrade of the Baileys npm package via npm/yarn/pnpm so the SOC can flag new vulnerable deployments and verify the chosen version is the patched 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12+. Complements the on-disk inventory hunt by catching introductions in real time. Rationale: Targets the exact package name strings (baileys, @whiskeysockets/baileys) from the advisory and the standard npm / yarn / pnpm install verbs. Catches new vulnerable deployments before they're hit, supplementing the on-disk inventory pivot. Cross-checked against the GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg affected-packages block. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@whiskeysockets/baileys
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate teams installing the patched 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc12+ version (analyst must check the version specifier in cmdline)
  • CI/CD pipeline runs that `npm install` baileys on every build
  • Developer workstations running `npm update` broadly across all deps
  • Dependabot/Renovate auto-PR scripts running `npm install` to validate
  • First-time install commands on a freshly bootstrapped repo
Suppression filter
// Exclude installs that explicitly pin a patched version
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "baileys@6.7.22"
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "baileys@7.0.0-rc12"
| where ProcessCommandLine !contains "baileys@latest"
// Exclude known build agents
| where DeviceName !has "ci-runner"
| where DeviceName !has "build-agent"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the captured cmdline — if it pins a patched version (`baileys@6.7.22`, `baileys@^7.0.0-rc12`, `baileys@latest` post-2026-06-10), close as benign. 2) Contain: if a vulnerable pin is being introduced, contact the developer/owner and have them re-pin to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 before merging. 3) Hunt: cross-reference DeviceName against UC1 inventory to confirm the on-disk version after the install completes; pivot to UC3 if this host runs a long-lived Baileys session.
// CVE-2026-48063 — Baileys npm install / upgrade hunt
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node")
    or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i ","update","upgrade")
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i ","update","upgrade")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// CVE-2026-48063 — Baileys npm install / upgrade hunt (ASIM)
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(npm|yarn|pnpm|node)(\.exe)?$"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install"," add "," i ","update","upgrade")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm/yarn/pnpm install or upgrade of Baileys package (CVE-2026-48063)
id: 7c2a4e8b-5d3f-4a1c-8e9b-2f6d4a8c1b3e
description: Detects package-manager command lines that install or upgrade the Baileys WhatsApp library — a vulnerable version (< 6.7.22 or 7.0.0-rc.1..rc11) introduces the placeholderResendMessage / messages.upsert spoofing flaw tracked as CVE-2026-48063.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg
author: detection-eng
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.001
  - cve.2026.48063
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '/npm'
      - '/yarn'
      - '/pnpm'
      - '/node'
  selection_pkg:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'baileys'
      - '@whiskeysockets/baileys'
  selection_action:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'install'
      - ' add '
      - ' i '
      - 'update'
      - 'upgrade'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_pkg and selection_action
level: medium
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:linux.auditd) (@Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\node.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/npm OR */yarn OR */pnpm OR */node)) (@CommandLine:*baileys* OR @process.command_line:*baileys*) (@CommandLine:(*install* OR *update* OR *upgrade* OR *" add "* OR *" i "*) OR @process.command_line:(*install* OR *update* OR *upgrade* OR *" add "* OR *" i "*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/(npm|yarn|pnpm|node)(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("baileys", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(install|update|upgrade|\\sadd\\s|\\si\\s)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node","npm-cli.js")) AND (Processes.process="*baileys*" OR Processes.process="*@whiskeysockets/baileys*") AND (Processes.process="*install*" OR Processes.process="* add *" OR Processes.process="* i *" OR Processes.process="*update*" OR Processes.process="*upgrade*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npm","yarn","pnpm","node","npm-cli.js")) AND (Processes.process="*baileys*" OR Processes.process="*@whiskeysockets/baileys*") AND (Processes.process="*install*" OR Processes.process="* add *" OR Processes.process="* i *" OR Processes.process="*update*" OR Processes.process="*upgrade*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Baileys messages.upsert event carrying a requestId field (exploit signature) AIActions on Objectives High
Direct exploit signature for CVE-2026-48063: the advisory's own workaround is to drop `messages.upsert` events that contain a `requestId` field — meaning that combination is the placeholderResendMessage abuse fingerprint. Hunts forwarded Node.js / Baileys application logs for that pairing on any host running the library. Rationale: Sourced directly from the advisory's workaround text: "dropping messages.upsert events that contain a requestId field" — i.e. Baileys' own maintainers identify the requestId-on-upsert pairing as the exploit signature. No detection guesswork; this is the article's named indicator. Defender Advanced Hunting has no general app-log table so defender_kql is left empty (call it out for SOC consumers running on Defender-only telemetry); Sigma is skipped because the detection needs a custom app-log logsource without a settled category. Falcon LogScale similarly only sees this if the consumer ships Node.js stdout to NG-SIEM ingest. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1565.001 T1566 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb Application
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Baileys debug logging enabled where `requestId` appears in unrelated socket protocol messages logged alongside (not actually on the upsert event) — verify the JSON nesting
  • Internal QA / red-team replay of historical exploit PoCs against staging Baileys instances
  • Patched Baileys (>= 6.7.22 / >= 7.0.0-rc12) re-logging dropped events for audit visibility — workaround behavior, not exploitation
  • Verbose log dumps where a single SyslogMessage line includes multiple unrelated event types and both strings coincidentally appear
Suppression filter
// Suppress patched-version hosts that may still log dropped events for visibility
| where Detail !has "dropped due to requestId"
| where Detail !has "workaround:placeholderResend"
// Suppress QA replay rigs
| where Computer !has "qa-baileys"
| where Computer !has "redteam-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the matching log line and confirm the `requestId` field is structurally inside the `messages.upsert` event object (not a separate adjacent log entry). Capture the spoofed message key, sender JID, and any payload. 2) Contain: if the host is on a vulnerable Baileys version (cross-ref UC1), upgrade immediately to 6.7.22 / 7.0.0-rc12 OR deploy the workaround (`shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false` + drop messages.upsert with requestId in the consumer). Treat any business decisions made on the basis of received WhatsApp messages on this host as untrusted from the time of first hit. 3) Hunt: pivot to all peer JIDs that received the spoofed upsert; check app-state-sync logs for cascading key-share or history-sync events around the same timestamp, since the same exploit also corrupts app state sync.
// CVE-2026-48063 — messages.upsert event with requestId field == placeholderResendMessage exploit signature
// Requires Baileys consumer apps to forward stdout/debug logs to Sentinel via Syslog or CEF
let baileys_exploit =
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SyslogMessage has "messages.upsert"
    | where SyslogMessage has "requestId"
    | extend Source = "Syslog"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Source, ProcessName, Detail = SyslogMessage;
let baileys_exploit_cef =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Message has "messages.upsert"
    | where Message has "requestId"
    | extend Source = "CommonSecurityLog"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DeviceExternalID, HostIP = SourceIP, Source, ProcessName, Detail = Message;
union baileys_exploit, baileys_exploit_cef
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:nodejs OR source:linux.syslog OR source:docker OR source:pm2) "messages.upsert" "requestId"
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype IN ("nodejs","node","pm2","syslog","linux:journald","linux_secure") OR source IN ("*baileys*","*whatsapp*")) ("messages.upsert" AND "requestId") AND ("placeholderResendMessage" OR "protocolMessage" OR "messages.upsert") | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(host) as hosts values(source) as sources by sourcetype | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48063")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48063")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48063")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48063")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

Code is being written everywhere, and the device is the only constant

Aikido
2026-06-10 7 use cases 2 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Developers are coding everywhere. AI agents, Slack bots, and MCP servers have made the developer device the biggest security blindspot. Category: News

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002
Domainsgiftshop.club sfrclak.com
IPs142.11.206.73 45.32.150.251 45.32.151.157 70.34.242.255
SHA12553649f23220496… d6f3f62fd3b9f543… 07d889e2dadce6f3…

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] NPM/Yarn/PNPM postinstall hook spawning credential-access tools · [LLM] Known SHA1 IOC from Aikido June-2026 supply chain advisory observed on endpoint · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Beaconing from developer endpoint to known TeamPCP/GlassWorm IOC infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Beaconing from developer endpoint to known TeamPCP/GlassWorm IOC infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunt for any DNS resolution or outbound connection from a corporate (developer) endpoint to the IPs/domains published alongside the Aikido June 2026 supply-chain advisory covering the TeamPCP, Axios maintainer hijack, GlassWorm VS Code extension, and malicious MCP server campaigns. High-fidelity because each indicator is a finished-intel atom — any single hit is worth a triage. Rationale: Anchors directly on the pre-extracted IOC list (4 IPv4s + 2 domains) shipped with the article. Each indicator is a single atom of finished intel — no behavioural inference required. Union'ed across Defender DeviceNetworkEvents, Sentinel DnsEvents/CommonSecurityLog/ImNetworkSession and Falcon DnsRequest/NetworkConnectIP4 so the same logic runs on whatever telemetry the tenant ships.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7) hitting the indicator list on a permitted-scan path — exclude scanner source IPs
  • Threat-intel proxy / sandbox detonation host that legitimately resolves IOCs as part of its job — exclude its hostname
  • Misconfigured DNS over HTTPS where 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8 returns parked-domain IP that collides with an IOC IP — verify via passive DNS
  • Legitimate research traffic from a security analyst's workstation to giftshop.club / sfrclak.com (rare but possible during triage of THIS very blog) — confirm via host tag = 'soc-research'
Suppression filter
// Defender refinement — drop known scanner/sandbox hosts
| where DeviceName !in~ ("tenable-scanner-01", "qualys-scanner-01", "soc-sandbox-01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessusd.exe", "qualysagent.exe", "cuckoo-agent.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the resolving process (`InitiatingProcessFileName`/`ContextImageFileName`), the user, and whether the host is on a known scanner/sandbox VLAN. Pivot on `DeviceId`/`aid` for any other IOC hits in the last 30 days, and check if the host has run `npm install`, `code --install-extension`, or pulled an MCP server in the same hour. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device via Defender/Falcon network containment; rotate any cloud/GitHub/npm credentials that were resident on the box (the article calls out AWS keys, SSH, npm publish tokens, kubeconfig); revoke active OAuth grants for the developer's identity. Step 3 — Hunt: search for the four IPs and two domains across all other endpoints + proxy logs for the same 30-day window; correlate with recent GitHub audit-log clones, npm `publish` actions, and any MCP/VS Code extension installs by the same user; sweep for the three SHA1 IOCs (see hash UC).
let IOC_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let IOC_Domains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where RemoteIP in (IOC_IPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (IOC_Domains)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Source="DeviceNetworkEvents"),
  (DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (IOC_Domains) or AdditionalFields has_any (IOC_IPs)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort=int(null), Source="DeviceEvents-Dns")
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOC_IPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let IOC_Domains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has_any (IOC_Domains) or RemoteIp in (IOC_IPs) or IPAddresses has_any (IOC_IPs)
    | extend Source = "DnsEvents", Host = Computer, DstIp = tostring(RemoteIp), DstHost = Name
    | project TimeGenerated, Source, Host, ClientIp = ClientIP, DstIp, DstHost),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP in (IOC_IPs) or DestinationHostName has_any (IOC_Domains) or DestinationDnsDomain has_any (IOC_Domains)
    | extend Source = "CommonSecurityLog", Host = DeviceName, ClientIp = SourceIP, DstIp = DestinationIP, DstHost = coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain)
    | project TimeGenerated, Source, Host, ClientIp, DstIp, DstHost),
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr in (IOC_IPs) or DstHostname has_any (IOC_Domains) or DstDomain has_any (IOC_Domains)
    | extend Source = "ImNetworkSession", Host = DvcHostname, ClientIp = SrcIpAddr, DstIp = DstIpAddr, DstHost = coalesce(DstHostname, DstDomain)
    | project TimeGenerated, Source, Host, ClientIp, DstIp, DstHost)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7b3e9c2a-4d8f-4a1e-9c5b-2f7e0a8d3b6c
description: Outbound network connection or DNS resolution to IPs/domains tied to the Aikido June 2026 supply chain advisory (TeamPCP / Axios maintainer hijack / GlassWorm / malicious MCP server campaigns).
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

  - attack.t1568
  - attack.command_and_control

  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp:
      - '142.11.206.73'
      - '45.32.150.251'
      - '45.32.151.157'
      - '70.34.242.255'
  selection_host:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'giftshop.club'
      - 'sfrclak.com'
  condition: selection_ip or selection_host
level: high
(source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR cloudtrail OR azure.activity_logs OR linux.auditd)) AND (@DestinationIp:("142.11.206.73" OR "45.32.150.251" OR "45.32.151.157" OR "70.34.242.255") OR @network.client.ip:("142.11.206.73" OR "45.32.150.251" OR "45.32.151.157" OR "70.34.242.255") OR @DestinationHostname:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*) OR @dns.question.name:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))

| RemoteAddressIP4=/^(142\.11\.206\.73|45\.32\.150\.251|45\.32\.151\.157|70\.34\.242\.255)$/ OR DomainName=/(^|\.)((giftshop\.club)|(sfrclak\.com))$/i OR FirstIP4Record=/^(142\.11\.206\.73|45\.32\.150\.251|45\.32\.151\.157|70\.34\.242\.255)$/

NPM/Yarn/PNPM postinstall hook spawning credential-access tools AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the exact scenario the article walks through: a developer approves a Slack-drafted PR, the agent merges and runs `npm install`, the postinstall hook then spawns a shell that reads AWS/SSH/.npmrc credentials or uploads them out. Looks for child processes of npm/yarn/pnpm/node/npx that touch credential paths or cloud-CLI verbs within a single install transaction. Rationale: The article spells the kill chain out plainly: 'agent merges the PR, pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook, and touches production credentials'. Anchors on the parent-process set (npm/yarn/pnpm/node/npx/corepack) plus a child set or cmdline grep that targets the credential paths and cloud-CLI verbs explicitly named in the article (cloud credentials, SSH keys, npm publish tokens, Kubernetes configs). Excludes machine accounts to cut CI noise.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AWS Amplify / serverless-framework projects whose postinstall legitimately runs `aws sts get-caller-identity` to confirm credentials
  • Legitimate publish scripts reading `.npmrc` to inject NPM_TOKEN during `npm publish`
  • Yarn berry installing native modules that shell out to `node-gyp` and download prebuilt binaries via curl/wget
  • Internal corp-bootstrap that copies `~/.aws/credentials` from a vault during `npm install` of an internal scaffold package
Suppression filter
// Defender refinement — drop known CI runners + signed bootstrap publishers
| where DeviceName !startswith "gh-runner-" and DeviceName !startswith "buildkite-"
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@corp/scaffold", "@corp/cli-bootstrap") and AccountName endswith "-svc")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full child-process tree under the originating `npm.exe` PID, capture the package name + version being installed (parent cmdline contains the registry URL), and check the npm-audit / package-lock for that version's publish age. If <72h old, treat as high suspicion. Step 2 — Contain: kill the process tree, quarantine the dependency from the corporate npm cache/mirror, freeze the developer's AWS keys / GitHub token / npm publish token (the four classes of credential the article calls out), and isolate the host if the child process reached the public internet. Step 3 — Hunt: search the org for any other endpoint that installed the same package@version; pivot on the package's npm publisher account and pull any other packages published from it in the same window; cross-reference with the IOC infrastructure UC for any C2 hits.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","corepack.exe")
| where (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"))
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\.aws\credentials", @"\.ssh\id_", @"\.npmrc", @"\.docker\config.json", @"kube\config", "aws s3 ", "aws iam ", "aws sts ", "Invoke-WebRequest", "DownloadString", "GITHUB_TOKEN", "NPM_TOKEN", "gh auth token")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let CredPathHints = dynamic([@"\.aws\credentials", @"\.ssh\id_", @"\.npmrc", @"\.docker\config.json", @"kube\config", "aws s3 ", "aws iam ", "aws sts ", "Invoke-WebRequest", "DownloadString", "GITHUB_TOKEN", "NPM_TOKEN", "gh auth token"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npx.exe","\\corepack.exe")
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe") or CommandLine has_any (CredPathHints)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, User=AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe","npx.exe","corepack.exe")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (CredPathHints)
    | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: NPM/Yarn Postinstall Hook Spawning Credential-Access Tooling

description: A node-ecosystem package manager (npm / yarn / pnpm / npx / corepack) spawns a shell, LOLBin, or command that touches developer credentials (.aws / .ssh / .npmrc / GitHub/NPM tokens). Matches the postinstall-hook abuse pattern called out in Aikido's June-2026 device-protection advisory.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) AND (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) AND @ParentImage:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\YARN.EXE OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\PNPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npx.exe OR *\\NPX.EXE OR *\\corepack.exe OR *\\COREPACK.EXE) AND (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\PWSH.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\WGET.EXE OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\CERTUTIL.EXE OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\BITSADMIN.EXE OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\BASH.EXE OR *\\sh.exe OR *\\SH.EXE) OR @CommandLine:(*.aws\\credentials* OR *.ssh\\id_* OR *.npmrc* OR *aws\ s3* OR *aws\ iam* OR *aws\ sts* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *DownloadString* OR *GITHUB_TOKEN* OR *NPM_TOKEN* OR *gh\ auth\ token*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|yarn|pnpm|node|npx|corepack)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin|bash|sh)\.exe$/i OR regex("\\\\\\.(aws\\\\credentials|ssh\\\\id_|npmrc|docker\\\\config\\.json)|kube\\\\config|aws (s3|iam|sts) |Invoke-WebRequest|DownloadString|GITHUB_TOKEN|NPM_TOKEN|gh auth token", field=CommandLine)
| UserName!=/\$$/

Malicious MCP server / node process opening outbound SMTP to non-corporate mail relay AIexfil Medium
Targets the September 2025 npm MCP-server backdoor the article cites — a node-hosted MCP server that BCC'd every outgoing email to an attacker mailbox. Hunts node.exe / pnpm-spawned node processes making direct SMTP/submission/IMAP connections to public IP space outside the sanctioned corporate mail relay set. Rationale: Article's concrete behavioural anchor for the MCP backdoor scenario: a node-hosted MCP server BCC-exfiltrating mail. Pivots on (node.exe) x (mail-protocol ports 25/465/587/2525/993/995) x (destination not in the sanctioned corporate relay set). Most legitimate Node apps don't speak SMTP/IMAP directly — they go through a corporate relay or transactional-mail API — so this combination is rare in healthy environments.
ATT&CKT1071.003 T1567 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer-laptop unit tests for a Nodemailer integration hitting Ethereal Email (ethereal.email) or Mailtrap sandbox endpoints
  • A SaaS product (Sendgrid/Mailgun/Postmark via raw SMTP) being legitimately used from a dev box during integration work
  • A node-based monitoring agent (e.g. Healthchecks) emailing alerts directly to a public mailbox by design
  • Self-hosted CI tools (Drone / Jenkins agent in node) using Gmail SMTP for build notifications when a corporate relay isn't configured
Suppression filter
// Defender refinement — drop dev-tool sandboxes
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("smtp.ethereal.email", "sandbox.smtp.mailtrap.io", "smtp.mailgun.org", "smtp.sendgrid.net", "smtp.postmarkapp.com"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the npm package the node process is hosting (walk the parent chain from node.exe up to npm.exe / pnpm.exe to recover the package path; inspect its package.json `bin` entry). Pull the package version and check publish age and publisher. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill the node process tree, block egress to the destination IPs at the perimeter, and rotate any mailbox / OAuth grant the MCP server had access to (especially Microsoft Graph Mail.Send / Mail.ReadWrite permissions). Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate every other endpoint that installed the same package@version; correlate with EmailEvents to see whether real customer mail was being shipped through this node process (check Sender mismatches between SenderFromAddress and the relay's account); pivot the destination IP against the IOC infrastructure UC.
let CorpMailRelays = dynamic(["smtp.corp.local","mail-relay-01.corp.local","outbound.protection.outlook.com","smtp.office365.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where RemotePort in (25, 465, 587, 2525, 993, 995)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any (CorpMailRelays))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Connections=count(), DistinctRemotes=dcount(RemoteIP), Remotes=make_set(RemoteIP, 20), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 20), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemotePort, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Connections > 0
| order by Timestamp desc
let CorpMailRelays = dynamic(["smtp.corp.local","mail-relay-01.corp.local","outbound.protection.outlook.com","smtp.office365.com"]);
let CorpRanges = dynamic(["10.","192.168.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31."]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (25, 465, 587, 2525, 993, 995)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe" or SrcProcessName has "node.exe"

| where not (DstIpAddr startswith_cs "10." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "192.168." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.16." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.17." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.18." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.19." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.20." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.21." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.22." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.23." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.24." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.25." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.26." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.27." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.28." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.29." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.30." or DstIpAddr startswith_cs "172.31.")

| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd OR windows.security) AND @EventID:3 AND @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR */node) AND @DestinationPort:(25 OR 465 OR 587 OR 2525 OR 993 OR 995) AND -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12) AND -@DestinationHostname:(*smtp.corp.local* OR *mail-relay-01.corp.local* OR *outbound.protection.outlook.com* OR *smtp.office365.com*)

Known SHA1 IOC from Aikido June-2026 supply chain advisory observed on endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Direct hash hit on any of the three SHA1 IOCs shipped with the Aikido device-protection advisory. Covers process execution, file write, and DLL/module load surfaces so the indicator catches whether the implant ran, was dropped to disk, or was loaded into another process. Rationale: Three concrete SHA1 atoms shipped with the article. Hash hits are essentially zero-FP — only collision risk is a known-good build coincidentally hashing identically (astronomically unlikely for SHA1 on full binaries). Covers process exec, file drop, and image-load surfaces so the indicator catches the implant whether it ran, was staged, or was side-loaded into another process.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR sandbox host detonating samples for IR purposes — exclude sandbox device names
  • Threat-hunter manually downloading the IOC for analysis on a research VM — confirm via user identity and host tag
  • Backup/archive scanner re-indexing an old quarantined sample — distinguish via initiating-process being the backup agent
  • False frontmatter in a corrupted file whose SHA1 accidentally collides with the IOC (vanishingly unlikely but worth noting before pulling the trigger on lateral search)
Suppression filter
// Exclude known SOC research / sandbox hosts
| where DeviceName !startswith "soc-sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "ir-research-" and DeviceName !startswith "detlab-"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the device is not a known sandbox / research VM. Pull the full process tree (parent → ancestor chain) and capture the file's on-disk path; check how it got there (npm install, VS Code extension install, browser download, Slack file share). Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host immediately; preserve a forensic image; freeze the developer's GitHub / npm / AWS / Slack OAuth grants; revoke active sessions for the user across SSO. Step 3 — Hunt: org-wide sweep on all three hashes across DeviceFileEvents / DeviceProcessEvents / DeviceImageLoadEvents going back 90 days; pivot on any npm package or VS Code extension installed in the hour preceding the hash hit; cross-check with the IOC infrastructure UC for any C2 connections from this device or any sibling devices; pull GitHub audit log for unusual clone/export activity by the user identity.
let IOC_SHA1 = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA1 in~ (IOC_SHA1)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, Cmdline=ProcessCommandLine, Source="DeviceProcessEvents"),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA1 in~ (IOC_SHA1)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, Cmdline=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="DeviceFileEvents"),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where SHA1 in~ (IOC_SHA1)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, Cmdline=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
let IOC_SHA1 = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where EventID == 4688 and FileHash has_any (IOC_SHA1)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, User=AccountName, FileName=NewProcessName, SHA1=FileHash, Cmdline=CommandLine, Source="SecurityEvent-4688"),
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where SHA1 in~ (IOC_SHA1)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, FileName=ActingProcessName, SHA1, Cmdline=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImProcessCreate"),
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileSHA1 in~ (IOC_SHA1)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, User=ActorUsername, FileName=TargetFileName, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1, Cmdline=ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImFileEvent"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where FileHash in~ (IOC_SHA1)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, User=SourceUserName, FileName, SHA1=FileHash, Cmdline=tostring(parse_json(EventData)), Source="CommonSecurityLog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cybersecurity researchers have warned of a "resurgence and expansion" of JDY, a covert network associated with China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors. "The JDY botnet comprises over 1,500 SOHO [small office and home office] and IoT devices and operates as a centrally controlled, high-performance scanner used to discover, fingerprint, and continuously map exposed services at scale," Lumen's

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] JDY-style outbound recon scanning originating from internal IoT / network appliances · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-35616 exploitation attempt against edge SOHO/IoT devices — JDY initial access · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MIPS shell-script dropper on Linux edge device — JDY architecture-aware payload fetch
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound Tor (9001/9030/9050) from network appliance / IoT subnet — JDY C2 beaconing · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
JDY-style outbound recon scanning originating from internal IoT / network appliances AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts internal SOHO routers, firewalls, and IoT devices behaving like JDY scanner bots — high-fanout outbound probes to public IPs across many service ports (TCP/SSL/UDP/ICMP) consistent with Black Lotus Labs' description of JDY's targeted fingerprinting role. Signal is a single internal source generating many distinct destination IPs in a short window — scanner-bot shape, not normal client behaviour. Rationale: Targets the specific JDY behaviour Black Lotus Labs described — high-volume outbound TCP/SSL/UDP/ICMP fingerprinting from compromised SOHO/IoT devices. Fan-out thresholds (200 distinct destinations, 5+ ports in 10 minutes) match scanner-bot shape, not normal client activity. CloudTrail has no telemetry for this — empty cloudwatch_query. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595/002/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable / Qualys / Rapid7) running an external attack-surface scan
  • DevOps health-check probe to 200+ partner endpoints from a single jumpbox
  • CDN / multiplayer game client opening hundreds of TURN/STUN connections
  • Backup software replicating to many cloud regions
  • SOC's own external Nmap/Masscan from a sanctioned host
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (lookup_table("sanctioned_scanners"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: pull the source host's asset record. Is it actually a SOHO router/IoT camera/NAS exposed to the public internet? Pivot on DeviceVendor/Model — Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, Draytek, Hikvision, Linksys are the named JDY-affected vendors. Check firmware against CVE-2026-35616. Step 2 — contain: isolate the device from internet egress (firewall block on management interface), capture a memory image if the platform supports it, notify owner. Step 3 — hunt: pivot the source IP across 30 days of perimeter logs for outbound Tor (9001/9030/9050), and search for short-lived MIPS-architecture binaries downloaded then self-deleted on peer devices of the same vendor.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionRequest")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","teams.exe","slack.exe")
| summarize DistinctDsts = dcount(RemoteIP), DistinctPorts = dcount(RemotePort), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 50), Protos = make_set(Protocol, 10), Hits = count() by DeviceName, DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctPorts >= 5  // JDY-style fan-out (Black Lotus Labs: high-volume TCP/SSL/UDP/ICMP probing)
| order by DistinctDsts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceAction in ("allow","accept","permit")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == true and ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| where isnotempty(DestinationPort)
| summarize DistinctDsts = dcount(DestinationIP), DistinctPorts = dcount(DestinationPort), Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 50), AppProtos = make_set(ApplicationProtocol, 10), Hits = count() by SourceIP, DeviceVendor, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctPorts >= 5  // JDY-style fan-out from internal IoT/SOHO source — empirical scanner-bot threshold
| order by DistinctDsts desc

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4

| ContextImageFileName!=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|outlook|teams|slack)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, bin(_time, 10m)], function=[count(as=Hits), count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctDsts), count(field=RemotePort, distinct=true, as=DistinctPorts)])

Outbound Tor (9001/9030/9050) from network appliance / IoT subnet — JDY C2 beaconing AICommand & Control High
JDY's architecture routes both C2 and payload-server traffic through Tor relays. Hunts outbound connections to well-known Tor ports (9001 OR, 9030 DirPort, 9050 SOCKS) from internal IPs in IoT/network-appliance segments. Network appliances and IP cameras have no business speaking Tor — even a single Tor connection from those segments is high-fidelity. Rationale: Three specific Tor ports (9001 OR, 9030 DirPort, 9050 SOCKS) named as JDY's C2 transport in the Black Lotus Labs writeup. Tor traffic from network-appliance / IoT subnets has near-zero legitimate baseline. CloudTrail has no Tor/network telemetry — empty cloudwatch_query is correct. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/003/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-research VM running a Tor browser on an analyst laptop that's misclassified as IoT segment
  • Privacy-aware end-user installing Tor browser intentionally
  • Researcher running an exit-node probe from a sanctioned testbed
  • Misconfigured P2P app reusing port 9001 (rare; verify with packet capture)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (lookup_table("sanctioned_tor_research"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: confirm source IP belongs to a managed device class (router/firewall/camera/NAS) and not a user endpoint that could legitimately run Tor browser. Pull recent firmware version + CVE-2026-35616 patch status. Step 2 — contain: firewall block all egress to the Tor destination IPs, then isolate the device from the corporate VLAN. Pull a config snapshot before powering off. Step 3 — hunt: pivot on the device's public IP — has it been receiving external probes? Cross-reference the destination Tor IPs against the Tor consensus relay list and Lumen JDY infra blocks; search for the same egress pattern from peer devices of the same vendor (vendor compromise wave).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050)  // Tor ORPort / DirPort / SOCKS — JDY uses Tor for C2 + payload (Black Lotus Labs)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort in (9001, 9030, 9050)  // Tor ORPort / DirPort / SOCKS
| where DeviceAction in ("allow","accept","permit")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == true and ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MIPS shell-script dropper on Linux edge device — JDY architecture-aware payload fetch AIInstallation High
The JDY dropper detects host CPU architecture (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) and fetches the matching binary, then deletes the binary from disk after launch. Hunts shell scripts on Linux/embedded edge devices that branch on uname/arch and invoke wget/curl/tftp followed by chmod +x and self-deletion. Rationale: Article explicitly names the JDY dropper's architecture detection (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) and its wget/curl-style payload fetch followed by self-deletion. Concrete strings + specific behaviour chain make this high-fidelity on Linux edge telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OpenWrt / DD-WRT firmware update script that branches on arch
  • Vendor OEM provisioning script for a new device
  • DevOps cross-compile pipeline detection script
  • Embedded-systems engineer manually installing a MIPS binary for testing
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: extract the URL the dropper fetched from and resolve it (likely Tor onion or short-lived IP). Pull the SHA256 of any binary written before deletion. Step 2 — contain: pull the device offline from the network, snapshot configuration, mount filesystem read-only for forensics. Step 3 — hunt: search the same URL/IP and any sibling MIPS hashes across the edge fleet — JDY operators wave-deploy across same-vendor devices. Cross-reference against Black Lotus Labs JDY IoCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("sh","ash","busybox","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mipsel","mips64","mipsel64")  // JDY architecture-aware dropper (Black Lotus Labs)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wget","curl","tftp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("user","daemon","auth","authpriv","kern")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("mipsel","mips64","mipsel64")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget","curl","tftp")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY MIPS Architecture Shell Dropper
id: a8b3c9d1-7e42-4a5b-9f8c-3d2e1b4a5c6d
description: Shell script on a Linux/embedded edge device branching on MIPS CPU architecture and fetching a payload via wget/curl/tftp. Matches JDY botnet dropper described by Lumen Black Lotus Labs.
references:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2

| regex("(mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(wget|curl|tftp)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())

CVE-2026-35616 exploitation attempt against edge SOHO/IoT devices — JDY initial access AIExploitation Medium
JDY operators weaponise newly disclosed edge-device vulnerabilities for initial access, with CVE-2026-35616 named explicitly in the article. Hunts vendor advisories and edge-device telemetry for exploit attempts targeting devices from the named vendor list (Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, Draytek, Hikvision, Linksys). Rationale: Article names CVE-2026-35616 as the JDY operators' delivery vector for the shell-script dropper. Combined with Black Lotus Labs' named-vendor list (Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, Draytek, Hikvision, Linksys) the asset filter is high-precision. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html • https://blog.lumen.com/black-lotus-labs/

| where SourceIP !in (lookup_table("sanctioned_scanners"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: confirm targeted device is actually one of the named vendor/model classes (Cisco RV320/RV325, Araknis, Mimosa, Ubiquiti, DrayTek, Hikvision, Linksys) and check firmware against the CVE-2026-35616 advisory. Step 2 — contain: if exploit attempt succeeded (HTTP 200 + subsequent outbound shell-script-style request), isolate the device, dump config, and rotate any shared credentials. Step 3 — hunt: pivot the attacker's source IP across 30 days of perimeter logs — JDY scanner bots probe before exploitation, so the same IP often shows wide-fanout TCP/SSL fingerprinting first.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-35616"
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where DeviceCategory in ("NetworkDevice","IoT") or Vendor in~ ("Cisco","Araknis","Mimosa","Ubiquiti","DrayTek","Hikvision","Linksys")) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, Vendor, Model, IsInternetFacing
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Cisco","Fortinet","PaloAlto","Snort","Suricata")
| where Message has "CVE-2026-35616" or DeviceEventClassID has "35616" or RequestURL has_any ("/cgi-bin/","/setup.cgi")
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == true
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, Message, Activity
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(cisco.asa OR paloalto OR fortinet OR snort OR suricata) ("CVE-2026-35616" OR @url:(*\/cgi-bin\/* OR *\/setup.cgi*))
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Web.url) as URLs values(Web.http_user_agent) as UAs from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*cgi-bin*" OR Web.url="*setup.cgi*" OR Web.url="*35616*") Web.dest_category IN ("soho","network_appliance","iot") earliest=-7d by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.url) as URLs values(Web.http_user_agent) as UAs from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*cgi-bin*" OR Web.url="*setup.cgi*" OR Web.url="*35616*") Web.dest_category IN ("soho","network_appliance","iot") earliest=-7d by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | sort - count

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 RCE via /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests targeting the Ivanti Sentry MICS configuration endpoint that watchTowr Labs identified as the exploitation path for CVE-2026-10520 (unauthenticated root RCE) and the related auth-bypass CVE-2026-10523. The pre-patch endpoint required no authentication, so any inbound request to this URL on an unpatched appliance is exploitation-grade signal. Rationale: Endpoint path is the exact string watchTowr Labs disclosed for CVE-2026-10520 exploitation, quoted in the article body. Ivanti's own patch notes (cited in article) confirm the fix added authentication in front of this endpoint, meaning pre-patch any request to it bypassed authn — making the URL a deterministic exploit indicator. Same URL family is the auth-bypass vector for CVE-2026-10523 per the article.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus / Qualys / Tenable) probing the appliance post-disclosure
  • Post-patch validation traffic from the IT/security team confirming the endpoint now returns the login redirect
  • Ivanti support running diagnostic requests via the customer's VPN
  • Synthetic uptime/health probes accidentally configured against this path
  • watchTowr's own PoC re-run inside a sanctioned purple-team exercise
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("10.20.30.40", "10.20.30.41")  // org-approved vulnerability-scanner IPs
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Tenable", "Rapid7")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on SourceIP — is it inside known scanner CIDRs or internal admin jump-host? Check HTTP status: 200/302 vs 401/403 (post-patch redirect to login is the expected benign signal). Pull the request body if WAF captured it; look for shell metacharacters or MICS config commands. 2. Contain: if SourceIP is unauthorised and response was 200, treat as confirmed RCE — isolate the Sentry appliance from the management network, snapshot for forensics, and rotate any AD/MDM credentials Sentry held. 3. Hunt: pivot on the appliance's outbound connections for 24h before/after for reverse-shell or staging tools; review SecurityEvent 4624/4672 across managed devices Sentry could reach laterally; check appliance for new local admin accounts created via the auth-bypass (CVE-2026-10523).
// Catches internal-origin exploitation (red-team / insider / lateral) since Defender does not see external attacker traffic to the appliance itself
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fortinet FortiSandbox WEB UI command injection (CVE-2026-25089) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for HTTP requests to FortiSandbox / FortiSandbox Cloud / FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI that carry shell-metacharacter payloads consistent with CWE-78 OS command injection. The article confirms unauthenticated attackers can trigger RCE via specifically crafted HTTP requests; without a published endpoint we pivot on the appliance hostname/SNI plus injection markers. Rationale: Article identifies FortiSandbox / FortiSandbox Cloud / FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI as the affected component for CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS 9.1) and quotes Fortinet's CWE-78 OS-command-injection language. Without a disclosed endpoint, hostname-scoping plus URL-encoded shell metacharacters is the cleanest hunting pivot. Fortinet PSIRT advisory cited inline corroborates the affected versions.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FortiSandbox WEB UI form submissions containing semicolons in policy descriptions or comments
  • Administrator copy-pasting sample IOCs containing shell characters into the UI's threat-search field
  • Browser auto-encoding of querystring values that legitimately contain pipes (e.g. filter expressions)
  • FortiAnalyzer / FortiManager API calls that legitimately use `|` as a delimiter in some endpoints
  • Vulnerability scanner fuzzing the WEB UI as part of authorised assessment
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("FortiManager", "FortiAnalyzer", "FortiCloud")
| where SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8")  // adjust to your management network CIDR if the UI is admin-only
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm DestinationHostName actually resolves to a FortiSandbox (not a coincidentally-named asset); pull the full RequestURL and decode any percent-encoding to see if the injection looks like a real OS command (`;id`, `|bash -i`, ``$(curl ...)``) vs benign UI noise. 2. Contain: if confirmed, block SourceIP at the perimeter, take the FortiSandbox out of the inline detonation chain (failover to backup or temporarily route to FortiGate-only inspection), and capture an appliance config snapshot. 3. Hunt: pivot on outbound connections from the FortiSandbox to non-Fortinet IPs in the prior 7 days; check for new files dropped in /var/www or /tmp on the appliance via Fortinet's CLI diagnostics; review FortiSandbox audit log for unauthenticated config changes.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(fortisandbox|fsa-[a-z0-9-]+)"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (";", "|", "$(", "`", "%3B", "%7C", "%24%28", "%60")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName matches regex @"(?i)(fortisandbox|fsa-[a-z0-9-]+)" or DeviceProduct =~ "FortiSandbox"
| where RequestURL has_any (";", "|", "$(", "`", "%3B", "%7C", "%24%28", "%60")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SAP NetWeaver SAML XML Signature Wrapping pattern (CVE-2026-44748) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for SAML responses POSTed to SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP SAML SP consumer endpoints carrying multiple <Signature> or <Assertion> elements — the structural fingerprint of an XML signature wrapping (XSW) attack exploiting CVE-2026-44748 (CVSS 9.9). Onapsis (cited in article) describes an authenticated low-privilege attacker tampering with identity information in signed XML. Rationale: Article cites Onapsis describing the exact attack — 'authenticated attacker with normal privileges obtain a valid signed message and send modified signed XML documents with tampered identity information' — which is textbook XML signature wrapping. SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP SAML SP consumer endpoints (/sap/saml2/sp/*) are the receiver. XSW payloads inflate body size because the attacker copies the original signed element and inserts a malicious twin; a request-body-size hunt is the cheapest proxy when WAF doesn't parse XML.
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SAML responses from IdPs that include large attribute statements (group memberships for users in hundreds of groups)
  • ADFS / Azure AD assertions with embedded certificates inflating payload size
  • Federated SSO flows that carry encrypted assertions (which are naturally larger)
  • Re-authentication after IdP cert rotation pushing fresh metadata
  • SAML logout requests that include all session indexes for long-lived sessions
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("ADFS", "PingFederate", "Okta")  // known IdPs commonly producing large legitimate assertions
| where cIP !in ("<known-IdP-egress-CIDR>")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the SAML body from WAF if available; count occurrences of `<ds:Signature>` and `<saml:Assertion>` — XSW payloads have 2+ of each, legitimate responses have one. Compare the Subject NameID in the signed assertion vs the unsigned/wrapper assertion. 2. Contain: if confirmed XSW, invalidate the attacker's resulting SAP session (SM04 or rdisp/scheduler kill), force re-auth on the targeted privileged account, and rotate the SAP service-provider signing key. 3. Hunt: pivot on SAP audit log (SM20) for any RFC, transaction, or table access by the impersonated identity in the prior hour; review IdP logs for the source account to confirm whether the attacker legitimately authenticated as a low-priv user before forging the higher-priv identity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/sap/saml2/sp/", "/saml2/sp/acs", "/sap/public/bc/saml")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe", "firefox.exe", "iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let SamlPaths = dynamic(["/sap/saml2/sp/","/saml2/sp/acs","/sap/public/bc/saml"]);
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any (SamlPaths)
| extend BodyBytes = tolong(csBytes)
| where BodyBytes > 8192   // typical SAML response ~ 4-6 KB; XSW payloads inflate body via duplicate <Signature>/<Assertion>
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUriStem, csMethod, BodyBytes, scStatus, csUserName, csUserAgent
| order by BodyBytes desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:awswaf) @http.method:POST (@http.url_details.path:*/sap/saml2/sp/* OR @http.url_details.path:*/saml2/sp/acs* OR @http.url_details.path:*/sap/public/bc/saml*) @http.request.body.bytes:>8192
# log group: /aws/elasticloadbalancing/<sap-netweaver-alb> (only if SAP NetWeaver fronted by AWS ALB)
fields @timestamp, client_ip, request_url, request_verb, request_processing_time, sent_bytes, received_bytes, elb_status_code, user_agent
| filter request_verb = "POST"
      and (request_url like /\/sap\/saml2\/sp\// or request_url like /\/saml2\/sp\/acs/ or request_url like /\/sap\/public\/bc\/saml/)
      and received_bytes > 8192
| sort received_bytes desc
| limit 200
